cards.explanation: The people are asking why no one talks of restoring the king. They say Absalom, the man they anointed, has died in battle. Then comes the question: “So why do you say nothing about restoring the king?” It's like a group chat that's been buzzing all day about one thing, and somebody finally types, "So are we actually gonna do something about this?"

The answer is Judah. David sends his message to Zadok and Abiathar, the priests, and it's for the elders of Judah. He asks why they should be the last to restore the king to his palace. Friends, I think the sting is in the word "last." Nobody wants to be last in line.

David tells the priests to remind the elders of Judah that they are his own flesh and blood. He says, “You are my brothers, my own flesh and blood.” Then he asks again why they should be the last to restore the king. He sounds like a man at a family reunion saying, "Come on, it's ME!"

The word is commander. David says, “…if from now on you are not the commander of my army in place of Joab!” Amasa, who led Absalom's army (2 Samuel 17:25), is being given Joab's place. That's a big wow, even for a stamper with a mustache.

The answer is False. The men of Judah are not split. The text says David “…swayed the hearts of all the men of Judah as though they were one man…” That's the opposite of split. They all sent word to the king with one voice.
The men of Judah send word to the king: “Return, you and all your servants.” Six words and the whole mood flips. After all that arguing, that's the sweetest text David could get.

The men of Judah come to Gilgal to escort the king across the Jordan. The text says they came “…to meet him and escort him across the Jordan.” They aren't waiting at home, they come out to the river. That's like showing up at the airport instead of texting "safe travels."
The answer is True. Shimei son of Gera, a Benjamite from Bahurim, came down along with a thousand men of Benjamin. He didn't come alone. That's a whole crowd at the river with him.

The one who rushes down is Ziba, the steward of the house of Saul. He came to the Jordan with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. That's thirty-six people if you count Ziba, which is a whole crowd heading for one river. He wasn't coming by himself.

When Shimei reaches the king, he falls down before him. The text says that when Shimei crossed the Jordan, he fell down before the king. No hiding, no hanging back. The man goes straight to the ground.

Shimei asks the king not to hold him guilty. He says, “My lord, do not hold me guilty, and do not remember your servant’s wrongdoing on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem.” He asks the king not to take it to heart. It's a hard thing to ask, and he asks it from the ground.
The answer is False. Shimei does not insist he did nothing wrong. He says, “For your servant knows that I have sinned…” No excuses, no spin. That's about the hardest sentence to say out loud.

The answer is False. Abishai son of Zeruiah, one of David's commanders (2 Samuel 18:2), asks, “Shouldn’t Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the LORD’s anointed?” He wants Shimei put to death. Mercy is David's answer, not Abishai's.

David says he knows that today he is king over Israel. He asks, “Am I not indeed aware that today I am king over Israel?” He's saying he knows what day it is. Friends, I think he doesn't want it to be the day somebody dies.
The word is die. The king says to Shimei, “You shall not die.” Shimei had fallen down before the king, and these are the words he gets. I think that's a sentence he'll remember for a long time.
The answer is True. After telling Shimei, “You shall not die,” the king swore an oath to him. A king's word, with an oath on top. That's the promise nailed down twice.
